title: The Basics
intro: These are the basic tools we may use without reproving them. Cite a label such as **T1 (SAS)** or **O2 (equal tangents)**, and check its hypotheses. A problem may specify a narrower list of allowed facts.

We work in the Euclidean plane. A triangle has three noncollinear vertices, and a circle has positive radius. **AB** denotes the length of the segment joining A and B. For distinct points A and B, the line through them extends in both directions. In **∠ABC**, B is the vertex. Angles are non-reflex and measured in degrees.

A definition does not itself establish existence or uniqueness. Use a converse when it is explicitly stated here. Diagrams illustrate the statements: an apparent equality, right angle, parallelism, or concurrence is not an additional hypothesis.

blocks.text: Through any point P there is exactly one line perpendicular to a given line ℓ. If P is not on ℓ, its intersection H with ℓ is the **foot of the perpendicular**, and PH is the distance from P to ℓ. A point on ℓ has distance zero from ℓ.
An **altitude** is the perpendicular drawn from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side. Its foot may lie on the side, at an endpoint, or beyond an endpoint.

figures.caption: Perpendicular foot and distance.
figures.alt: Point P lies above line ell. PH is perpendicular to ell, and H is the perpendicular foot.

figures.caption: An altitude outside the triangle.
figures.alt: Triangle ABC is obtuse at B. The perpendicular from A to the line BC has foot H outside the segment BC.

blocks.text: A **rigid motion**, or **isometry**, is a bijection of the plane that preserves distances. We may apply translations, rotations, reflections, and their compositions. Every point of a figure moves by the same motion.

Rigid motions take lines to lines, segments to segments, and circles to circles. They preserve angles, betweenness, parallelism, perpendicularity, and area. A reflection may reverse a figure's orientation.
Two figures are **congruent** if a rigid motion carries one onto the other. Corresponding lengths and angles are equal.

figures.caption: Translation of a triangle.
figures.alt: The same horizontal translation takes A, B and C to A prime, B prime and C prime. The two triangles have equal corresponding lengths and angles.

figures.caption: Rotation through a right angle.
figures.alt: A quarter turn counterclockwise about O takes triangle ABC to triangle A prime B prime C prime.

figures.caption: Reflection across a line.
figures.alt: Reflection across the vertical line ell takes each vertex to the corresponding prime vertex and reverses the orientation of the triangle.

blocks.text: A **similitude** of scale factor k > 0 is a bijection S of the plane satisfying **S(A)S(B) = k·AB** for every pair A, B.
A **dilation** with center O and factor k > 0 fixes O and sends P ≠ O to the point P′ on ray OP with **OP′ = k·OP**. We may apply dilations and compose them with rigid motions.

Similitudes preserve angles, betweenness, parallelism, and perpendicularity. Lengths are multiplied by **k**, and polygon areas by **k²**. Two figures are **similar** if a similitude carries one onto the other. A scale factor of 1 gives a rigid motion.

figures.caption: Dilation about a center.
figures.alt: A dilation about O with scale factor two takes ABC to A prime B prime C prime. Corresponding points lie on the same rays from O. In general lengths multiply by k and areas by k squared.

items: **Rectangle:** area = bh for side lengths b and h.
**Triangle:** area = ½bh, where h is the perpendicular distance from the opposite vertex to the line containing the base of length b. The foot of the altitude may lie outside the side.
**Additivity:** if a polygon is partitioned into finitely many polygonal pieces with disjoint interiors, its area is the sum of their areas. The polygonal boundaries contribute no area.
**Comparison:** triangles with equal bases and equal heights have equal areas. With a common height, their areas have the same ratio as their base lengths.

blocks.text: Rigid motions preserve area.

figures.caption: Area of a rectangle.
figures.alt: A rectangle with base b and perpendicular height h has area b times h.

figures.caption: Area with an exterior altitude.
figures.alt: The chosen base BC has length b. The perpendicular height h is AH, whose foot H lies outside BC. The area is one half b times h.

figures.caption: Equal bases and equal heights.
figures.alt: Two triangles lie between the same parallel horizontal lines. Their base lengths are both b and their heights are both h, so their areas are equal.

figures.caption: Common height and area ratio.
figures.alt: Two triangles have a common perpendicular height h. Their area ratio equals the ratio of their base lengths b one and b two.

figures.caption: Adding the areas of polygonal pieces.
figures.alt: Two diagonals divide a convex pentagon into three triangles with disjoint interiors. The area of the pentagon is the sum of the three areas.

blocks.text: A **right angle** measures 90°; a **straight angle** measures 180°. Adjacent angles that form a straight angle add to **180°**.
When two distinct lines intersect, opposite (**vertical**) angles are equal. Adjacent angles need not be equal.

figures.caption: A right angle.
figures.alt: Two perpendicular rays form a right angle of ninety degrees.

figures.caption: Adjacent angles on a straight line.
figures.alt: Two adjacent angles alpha and beta fill a straight angle, so their measures sum to one hundred eighty degrees.

figures.caption: Vertical angles.
figures.alt: Two intersecting lines form two equal opposite alpha angles and two equal opposite beta angles. Adjacent alpha and beta angles are not marked equal.

blocks.text: **△ABC ≅ △DEF** specifies A ↔ D, B ↔ E, C ↔ F. Congruent triangles have equal corresponding side lengths and angle measures. Each test below establishes congruence.

items: **SAS:** two corresponding sides and their **included angle** are equal.
**SSS:** all three corresponding sides are equal.
**ASA:** two corresponding angles and their **included side** are equal.
**HL:** both triangles are right triangles, their hypotenuses are equal, and one pair of corresponding legs is equal. The hypotenuse lies opposite the right angle.
**Two angles and a side:** two corresponding angles and any one corresponding side are equal.

blocks.text: Two sides and a non-included angle (**SSA**) do not in general establish congruence.
**Isosceles triangle theorem and converse.** An isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides. In △ABC,
**AB = AC ⇔ ∠ABC = ∠ACB.**
Equal sides give equal base angles; equal base angles give equal sides.

figures.caption: SAS congruence.
figures.alt: The corresponding sides AB and DE have one tick. AC and DF have two ticks. The included angles at A and D are equal. The correspondence is A to D, B to E, and C to F.

figures.caption: SSS congruence.
figures.alt: All three pairs of corresponding sides are marked equal using one, two, and three ticks. The correspondence is A to D, B to E, and C to F.

figures.caption: ASA congruence.
figures.alt: The angles at A and D have one arc, the angles at B and E have two arcs, and the included sides AB and DE have matching ticks. The correspondence is A to D, B to E, and C to F.

figures.caption: Two angles and a non-included side.
figures.alt: The angles at A and D have one arc, the angles at B and E have two arcs, and the non-included sides BC and EF have matching ticks. The correspondence is A to D, B to E, and C to F.

figures.caption: Hypotenuse-leg congruence.
figures.alt: Both triangles have right angles at A and D. Their hypotenuses BC and EF and legs AB and DE are marked equal. The correspondence is A to D, B to E, and C to F.

figures.caption: Equal sides and equal base angles.
figures.alt: Triangle ABC has AB equal to AC. The equal angles opposite these sides are the base angles at B and C. The equivalence also works in reverse.

blocks.text: The interior angles of a triangle add to **180°**:
If BC is extended through C to D, with B, C, D in that order, then
**∠ACD = ∠BAC + ∠ABC.**
An exterior angle is greater than either of its two remote interior angles.

figures.caption: Angles in a triangle.
figures.alt: The three interior angles alpha, beta and gamma of triangle ABC sum to one hundred eighty degrees.

figures.caption: Exterior angle of a triangle.
figures.alt: Side BC continues through C to D. The exterior angle theta at C is the sum of the remote interior angles alpha at A and beta at B.

blocks.text: Within one triangle, a greater side lies opposite a greater angle, and conversely. Equal sides lie opposite equal angles, and conversely:
**AB > AC ⇔ ∠ACB > ∠ABC,**
**AB = AC ⇔ ∠ACB = ∠ABC.**
These comparisons concern sides and angles of the **same triangle**.

figures.caption: Comparing opposite sides and angles.
figures.alt: In this triangle AB is longer than AC. The opposite angle gamma at C is greater than beta at B. The side and angle comparisons are equivalent.

blocks.text: Each side of a triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two. In particular,
**AB < AC + CB**, and **|AB − AC| < BC < AB + AC**.
For any three points, **AB ≤ AC + CB**. Equality holds exactly when C lies on the closed segment from A to B, including either endpoint. A nondegenerate triangle gives strict inequality.

figures.caption: Strict triangle inequality.
figures.alt: The direct side AB is shorter than the two sides AC and CB together in a nondegenerate triangle.

figures.caption: Equality for collinear points.
figures.alt: Point C lies on segment AB between A and B. Therefore the length AB equals AC plus CB.

blocks.text: Two equal pairs of corresponding angles establish triangle similarity. This is **AA**, equivalently **AAA**.
For **△ABC ∼ △DEF**, the correspondence is A ↔ D, B ↔ E, C ↔ F, and
**DE/AB = EF/BC = FD/CA = k > 0.**
The area of △DEF is **k²** times the area of △ABC. Equal corresponding angles do not by themselves give congruence: the scale factor need not be 1.

figures.caption: Similar triangles and scale.
figures.alt: Triangles ABC and DEF have equal corresponding angles. The displayed scale factor from ABC to DEF is three halves. All lengths multiply by k and all areas by k squared.

blocks.text: In a right triangle with leg lengths a, b and hypotenuse length c,
**a² + b² = c².**
Conversely, if a triangle has side lengths a, b, c satisfying this equation, its angle opposite c is a right angle.

figures.caption: Pythagoras and its converse.
figures.alt: A right triangle has legs a and b and hypotenuse c. The equation a squared plus b squared equals c squared characterizes a right angle opposite c.

blocks.text: Two distinct lines are **parallel** if they do not meet. A **transversal** meets two distinct lines at different points. At either intersection, interior angles have a side along the transversal pointing toward the other intersection. An alternate interior pair contains one such angle at each intersection, on opposite sides of the transversal.
If the lines are parallel, alternate interior angles are equal. Conversely, equality of a pair of alternate interior angles establishes parallelism.
The “Z” identifies the angle pair; its appearance alone does not establish parallelism.

figures.caption: Alternate interior angles.
figures.alt: Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by a sloping transversal. The angle below the upper line and left of the transversal, and the angle above the lower line and right of the transversal, are both marked alpha.

blocks.text: For two parallel lines cut by a transversal:

items: **Corresponding angles**, in matching positions at the two intersections, are equal.

blocks.text: Both converses are allowed: an equal corresponding pair, or a same-side interior pair with sum 180°, establishes parallelism.

figures.caption: Corresponding angles.
figures.alt: Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by a sloping transversal. At each crossing the angle above the parallel line and right of the transversal is marked alpha.

figures.caption: Same-side interior angles.
figures.alt: Two parallel horizontal lines are crossed by a sloping transversal. The two interior angles on the right of the transversal are marked alpha and beta, with alpha plus beta equal to 180 degrees.

blocks.text: A **tangent** is a line that meets a circle in exactly one point, its **point of tangency**.
For a circle with center O, a line tangent at T is perpendicular to **OT**. Conversely, if T lies on the circle, the line through T perpendicular to OT is tangent there.
There is exactly one tangent at each point of a circle. The radius and tangent meet at that point of tangency.

figures.caption: A radius perpendicular to a tangent.
figures.alt: A circle with center O meets a vertical tangent line at T. The radius OT and the tangent form a marked right angle.

blocks.text: From a point P strictly outside a circle with center O, there are exactly two tangent lines. If they touch the circle at A and B, then
**PA = PB.**
Both segments start at the **same exterior point** and end at points of tangency on the **same circle**. The radii OA and OB are perpendicular to PA and PB, respectively.
For a circle of center O and radius r, the number of tangent lines through P is:

figures.caption: Equal tangent segments from an exterior point.
figures.alt: The two segments PA and PB touch a circle at A and B. Matching marks show that PA and PB have equal lengths. Dashed radii OA and OB each meet the corresponding tangent at a marked right angle.

figures.caption: On the circle: one tangent. Inside: no tangents; the drawn lines are secants.
figures.alt: Left: P lies on the circle and has one tangent. Right: P lies inside the circle. Each of the two drawn lines through P crosses the circle at two marked points, so both lines are secants; no tangent passes through P.
